claim: Current methods do not enable precise engineering of complex genotypes that can be easily tracked in a mixed population of cells.
source: Current methods do not enable precise engineering of complex genotypes that can be easily tracked in a mixed population of cells.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations of existing methods presented in the abstract without specific experimental data or citations in this sentence.

claim: The method combines rAAV6 donor delivery and the CRISPR/Cas9 system delivered as ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) to multiplex homologous recombination in human hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells and primary human T cells.
source: We describe a method to multiplex homologous recombination (HR) in human hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells and primary human T cells by combining rAAV6 donor delivery and the CRISPR/Cas9 system delivered as ribonucleoproteins (RNPs).
evidence: This describes the methodology developed in the study, which is supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The use of reporter genes allows FACS-purification and tracking of cells that have had multiple alleles or loci modified by HR.
source: In addition, the use of reporter genes allows FACS-purification and tracking of cells that have had multiple alleles or loci modified by HR.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing FACS sorting and tracking of reporter-positive cells throughout the manuscript.

claim: Lentiviral-based overexpression or RNAi-mediated knockdown are the current gold standard methods for studying human hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell gene function.
source: The current gold standard method for studying human hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell (HSPC) gene function has been either overexpression or RNAi-mediated knockdown of genes using lentiviral vectors (Doulatov et al., 2012; Chan et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Lentiviral methods have confounders including random integration of the vector into the host genome, unregulated transgene expression, and incomplete gene knockdown.
source: While these methods have provided great insights into HSPC biology, they come with several confounders, such as random integration of the vector into the host genome, unregulated transgene expression, and incomplete gene knockdown (Woods et al., 2006; Naldini, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature describing limitations of lentiviral methods.

claim: Programmable nucleases such as ZFNs, TALENs, and CRISPR/Cas9 have been utilized to disrupt genes by introducing site-specific DNA double strand breaks that are corrected through NHEJ.
source: More recently, programmable nucleases such as zinc finger nucleases (ZFNs), transcription activator-like effector nucleases (TALENs), and CRISPR/Cas9 have been utilized to disrupt genes by the introduction of site-specific DNA double strand breaks (DSBs) that are corrected through non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) (Hendel et al., 2015; Holt et al., 2010; Saydaminova et al., 2015; Mandal et al., 2014; Schumann et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2014; Lin et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: NHEJ creates a heterogeneous mixture of cells with various genotypes of SNPs and small insertions or deletions (INDELs).
source: This error-prone system creates a heterogeneous mixture of cells with various genotypes of SNPs and small insertions or deletions (INDELs); moreover, not all of the genetic changes from INDELs cause functional gene disruption as they may preserve the open reading frame and may not change amino acids essential for protein functions (Shi et al., 2015; Hultquist et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature describing NHEJ outcomes.

claim: Not all genetic changes from INDELs cause functional gene disruption as they may preserve the open reading frame and may not change amino acids essential for protein functions.
source: This error-prone system creates a heterogeneous mixture of cells with various genotypes of SNPs and small insertions or deletions (INDELs); moreover, not all of the genetic changes from INDELs cause functional gene disruption as they may preserve the open reading frame and may not change amino acids essential for protein functions (Shi et al., 2015; Hultquist et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A prior study created defined gene deletions in HSPCs using a dual sgRNA approach, but more than half of the alleles were not modified leading to residual gene expression.
source: In a prior study, defined gene deletions were created in HSPCs using a dual sgRNA approach, however, more than half of the alleles were not modified leading to residual gene expression (Mandal et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Successfully modified cells in the prior study were not distinguishable from unmodified wild type cells and could not be tracked or isolated as an enriched population.
source: Another limitation of this prior study is that successfully modified cells were not distinguishable from unmodified wild type (WT) cells, and therefore could not be tracked or isolated as an enriched population.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the cited prior study's methodology.

claim: Multiplexing of NHEJ-based gene editing has mainly been performed in immortalized human cancer cell lines and mouse cells.
source: Although the versatility of the CRISPR/Cas9 system allows for simultaneous manipulation at multiple genetic loci in a single cell, multiplexing of NHEJ-based gene editing has mainly been performed in immortalized human cancer cell lines and mouse cells (Hultquist et al., 2016; Cong et al., 2013; Heckl et al., 2014; Platt et al., 2014; Brown et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Prior multiplexed proof-of-concept studies only used NHEJ-mediated editing and did not harness the power of homologous recombination to create more sophisticated alterations to the genome at multiple alleles and/or loci.
source: Finally, these interesting multiplexed proof-of-concept studies, only used NHEJ-mediated editing and did not harness the power of homologous recombination (HR) to create more sophisticated alterations to the genome at multiple alleles and/or loci.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the cited prior studies' methodologies.

claim: HR in human HSPCs can be efficiently induced by site-specific nucleases in combination with homologous donor DNA delivered as ssODNs, IDLVs, or rAAV6 vectors.
source: We and others have previously shown that HR in human HSPCs can be efficiently induced by site-specific nucleases in combination with homologous donor DNA delivered as single-stranded oligonucleotides (ssODNs), integration-defective lentiviral vectors (ÍDLVs), or by recombinant adeno-associated virus serotype 6 (rAAV6) vectors (Dever et al., 2016; DeWitt et al., 2016; De Ravin et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2015; Hoban et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature including the authors' own work.

claim: Targeted integration in the beta-globin gene (HBB) was previously achieved by combining delivery of Cas9 protein pre-complexed with chemically modified sgRNAs (RNP) and delivery of an AAV6 donor.
source: We previously showed targeted integration in the beta-globin gene (HBB) by combining delivery of Cas9 protein pre-complexed with chemically modified sgRNAs (RNP) and delivery of an AAV6 donor.
evidence: This claim refers to the authors' prior published work.

claim: FACS-based sorting of transgene reporter-high-expressing HSPCs was used to purify an HSPC population with >90% targeted integration that displayed long-term repopulation capacity in NSG mice.
source: After successful on-target integration of a reporter transgene, FACS-based sorting of transgene reporterhigh-expressing HSPCs was used to purify an HSPC population with >90% targeted integration that displayed long-term repopulation capacity in NSG mice (Dever et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' prior work.

claim: Six additional loci (IL2RG, CCR5, RUNX1c, ASXL1, STAG2, and AAVS1) were tested for their potential to be modified through HR by CRISPR/Cas9 in combination with AAV6-derived donor delivery.
source: To extend this method beyond the HBB locus for therapeutic genome editing approaches of hemoglobinopathies, we tested six additional loci for their potential to be modified through HR by CRISPR/Cas9 in combination with AAV6-derived donor delivery. These genes are associated with hematopoiesis, hematopoietic malignancies, or safe harbor sites and include: interleukin-2 receptor gamma chain (IL2RG), chemokine (C-C motif) receptor 5 (CCR5), runt-related transcription factor one isoform c (RUNX1c), additional sex combs like 1 (ASXL1), stromal antigen 2 (STAG2), and adeno-associated virus integration site 1 (AAVS1) (Tebas et al., 2014; Genovese et al., 2014; Patel et al., 2012; Mazumdar et al., 2015; Kotin et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in the manuscript and citations for gene associations.

claim: Following electroporation with Cas9 RNP and transduction with an rAAV6 donor vector, a cell population with increased fluorescence intensity (reporterhigh cells) was detectable by flow cytometry at day 4 compared to cells receiving only the rAAV6 donor without electroporation of Cas9 RNP.
source: Following electroporation with Cas9 RNP, containing a chemically-modified sgRNA targeting a single site in the selected locus, and transduction with an rAAV6 donor vector carrying homology arms for the targeted site and an expression cassette encoding a fluorescent reporter gene (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a), we observed at early time points (day 4) a cell population with increased fluorescence intensity detectable by flow cytometry (reporterhigh cells) compared to cells receiving only the rAAV6 donor without electroporation of Cas9 RNP (reporterlow) (Figure 1a and Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a and Supplementary file 1a.

claim: Reporterhigh populations remained 99.2 ± 0.7% reporter positive after sorting at day four post-electroporation and culturing up to 22 days.
source: Reporterhigh populations remained 99.2 ± 0.7% reporter positive (Figure 1b) while sorted reporterlow and reporterneg populations were 29.3 ± 5.4% and 0.6 ± 0.2% reporter positive, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Sorted reporterlow populations were 29.3 ± 5.4% reporter positive after culturing.
source: Reporterhigh populations remained 99.2 ± 0.7% reporter positive (Figure 1b) while sorted reporterlow and reporterneg populations were 29.3 ± 5.4% and 0.6 ± 0.2% reporter positive, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Sorted reporterneg populations were 0.6 ± 0.2% reporter positive after culturing.
source: Reporterhigh populations remained 99.2 ± 0.7% reporter positive (Figure 1b) while sorted reporterlow and reporterneg populations were 29.3 ± 5.4% and 0.6 ± 0.2% reporter positive, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: GFP intensity at day four post-electroporation positively correlated with the propensity for maintaining GFP expression at day 20.
source: Dividing the reporterlow cells into three sub fractions based on fluorescence intensity revealed that GFP intensity at day four post-electroporation positively correlated with the propensity for maintaining GFP expression at day 20 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b–c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b–c.

claim: Targeted HSPCs formed a mix of myeloid (CFU-M/GM) and erythroid colonies (BFU-E, CFU-E) indicating that they retained HSPC function.
source: Targeted HSPCs formed a mix of myeloid (CFU-M/GM) and erythroid colonies (BFU-E, CFU-E) indicating that they retained HSPC function.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from methylcellulose colony assays.

claim: 99% of reporterhigh HSPCs targeted at CCR5 (338 clones analyzed) had at least a monoallelic targeted integration.
source: 'In-Out PCR' (one donor-specific primer and one locus-specific primer outside of the respective homology arms) on genomic DNA (gDNA) from single cell-derived methylcellulose colonies confirmed that 99%, 92%, and 100% of reporterhigh HSPCs targeted at CCR5 (338 clones analyzed), IL2RG (117 clones analyzed), and RUNX1 (36 clones analyzed), respectively, had at least a monoallelic targeted integration (Figure 1c and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCR genotyping data shown in Figure 1c and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: 92% of reporterhigh HSPCs targeted at IL2RG (117 clones analyzed) had at least a monoallelic targeted integration.
source: 'In-Out PCR' (one donor-specific primer and one locus-specific primer outside of the respective homology arms) on genomic DNA (gDNA) from single cell-derived methylcellulose colonies confirmed that 99%, 92%, and 100% of reporterhigh HSPCs targeted at CCR5 (338 clones analyzed), IL2RG (117 clones analyzed), and RUNX1 (36 clones analyzed), respectively, had at least a monoallelic targeted integration (Figure 1c and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCR genotyping data shown in Figure 1c and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: 100% of reporterhigh HSPCs targeted at RUNX1 (36 clones analyzed) had at least a monoallelic targeted integration.
source: 'In-Out PCR' (one donor-specific primer and one locus-specific primer outside of the respective homology arms) on genomic DNA (gDNA) from single cell-derived methylcellulose colonies confirmed that 99%, 92%, and 100% of reporterhigh HSPCs targeted at CCR5 (338 clones analyzed), IL2RG (117 clones analyzed), and RUNX1 (36 clones analyzed), respectively, had at least a monoallelic targeted integration (Figure 1c and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCR genotyping data shown in Figure 1c and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Analyses of clones with only mono-allelic integration showed gene-specific differences in the modification of the non-integrated alleles ranging from 38% INDELs for IL2RG to 89% INDELs for CCR5 and 88% INDELs for RUNX1.
source: Analyses of clones with only mono-allelic integration showed gene-specific differences in the modification of the non-integrated alleles ranging from 38% INDELs for IL2RG to 89% INDELs for CCR5% and 88% INDELs for RUNX1, among which the majority was gene-disrupting (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 1b.

claim: The majority of INDELs on non-integrated alleles were gene-disrupting.
source: Analyses of clones with only mono-allelic integration showed gene-specific differences in the modification of the non-integrated alleles ranging from 38% INDELs for IL2RG to 89% INDELs for CCR5% and 88% INDELs for RUNX1, among which the majority was gene-disrupting (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 1b.

claim: The observed log-fold transgene expression shift following rAAV6 and RNP delivery is due to HR at the intended locus.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that the observed log-fold transgene expression shift following rAAV6 and RNP delivery is due to HR at the intended locus and that reporter expression can be used to enrich gene-targeted HSPCs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing correlation between reporter expression and confirmed targeted integration.

claim: Reporter expression can be used to enrich gene-targeted HSPCs.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that the observed log-fold transgene expression shift following rAAV6 and RNP delivery is due to HR at the intended locus and that reporter expression can be used to enrich gene-targeted HSPCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing high purity of targeted integration in sorted reporter-high cells.

claim: The cohesin complex has previously been shown to play an essential part in maintaining normal erythroid differentiation potential of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells.
source: The cohesin complex has previously been shown to play an essential part in maintaining normal erythroid differentiation potential of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (Mazumdar et al., 2015; Viny et al., 2015; Mullenders et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The STAG2 gene is located on the human X chromosome.
source: Since the STAG2 gene is located on the human X chromosome, single-allele integration of a fluorescent reporter in male cells would be sufficient to fully knock out the gene.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the chromosomal location of STAG2.

claim: Single-allele integration of a fluorescent reporter in male cells would be sufficient to fully knock out the STAG2 gene.
source: Since the STAG2 gene is located on the human X chromosome, single-allele integration of a fluorescent reporter in male cells would be sufficient to fully knock out the gene.
evidence: This is inferred from the knowledge that males have only one X chromosome.

claim: Cas9 RNP combined with rAAV6 donor transduction resulted in the generation of a reporterhigh population for STAG2 targeting.
source: As expected, Cas9 RNP combined with rAAV6 donor transduction resulted in the generation of a reporterhigh population that could be sorted for subsequent differentiation experiments.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the STAG2 targeting experiments.

claim: Single cell methylcellulose assays of STAG2 reporterhigh cells revealed an almost complete loss in the capacity to form erythroid colonies compared to cells that had only been exposed to rAAV6 and not Cas9 RNP.
source: Single cell methylcellulose assays of reporterhigh cells revealed an almost complete loss in the capacity to form erythroid colonies compared to cells that had only been exposed to rAAV6 and not Cas9 RNP, and also compared to cells with targeted integration at the AAVS1 locus (Figure 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: STAG2 reporterhigh cells showed an almost complete loss in the capacity to form erythroid colonies compared to cells with targeted integration at the AAVS1 locus.
source: Single cell methylcellulose assays of reporterhigh cells revealed an almost complete loss in the capacity to form erythroid colonies compared to cells that had only been exposed to rAAV6 and not Cas9 RNP, and also compared to cells with targeted integration at the AAVS1 locus (Figure 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Gene-specific enrichment of reporterhigh cells can be used to study HSPC gene function.
source: These proof-of-concept studies provide evidence that gene-specific enrichment of reporterhigh cells can be used to study HSPC gene function.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the STAG2 functional study demonstrating loss of erythroid differentiation.

claim: Targeting the ASXL1 gene with GFP and BFP-encoding rAAV6 donors resulted in 10.4% of cells being double positive for GFPhigh and BFPhigh four days after electroporation and transduction.
source: To determine if this method could be used to enrich HSPCs with biallelic gene disruption, necessary for complete functional gene knockout, we targeted the ASXL1 gene and simultaneously provided GFP and BFP-encoding rAAV6 donors. Four days after electroporation and transduction, 10.4% of cells were double positive for GFPhigh and BFPhigh compared to 0.2% for the AAV only sample (Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: AAV only samples showed 0.2% double positive cells for GFPhigh and BFPhigh.
source: Four days after electroporation and transduction, 10.4% of cells were double positive for GFPhigh and BFPhigh compared to 0.2% for the AAV only sample (Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Double-positive populations were apparent when targeting three other genes (RUNX1, HBB, and CCR5) with two rAAV6 donors with various color combinations.
source: Similarly, double-positive populations were apparent when targeting three other genes (RUNX1, HBB, and CCR5) with two rAAV6 donors with various color combinations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1c.

claim: 'In-out PCR' on gDNA from single cell-derived methylcellulose clones confirmed on-target integration of one transgene into one allele and the other transgene into the second allele.
source: 'In-out PCR' on gDNA from single cell-derived methylcellulose clones confirmed on-target integration of one transgene into one allele and the other transgene into the second allele (Figure 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCR genotyping data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Primary human T cells can be targeted for biallelic HR at CCR5.
source: We next tested if the biallelic targeting approach could be extended to another blood cell type and therefore targeted primary human T cells for biallelic HR at CCR5. After electroporation with CCR5-targeting Cas9 RNP followed by transduction with GFP and mCherry CCR5 rAAV6 donors, a GFPhigh/mCherryhigh double-positive population was observed, indicative of biallelic integration at the CCR5 gene (Figure 2d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: No significant toxicity was associated with biallelic targeting in T cells.
source: No significant toxicity was associated with biallelic targeting in T cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by viability data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Human HSPCs and T cells that have undergone biallelic homologous recombination can be enriched using rAAV6, Cas9 RNP, and FACS.
source: Overall, these results demonstrate the utility of using rAAV6, Cas9 RNP, and FACS to enrich for primary human HSPCs and T cells that have undergone biallelic homologous recombination, which may have applications for studying hematological and immunological diseases or generating HSPC or T cell therapeutics that require gene modifications or gene knockout at both alleles.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data demonstrating biallelic targeting in HSPCs and T cells.

claim: Co-delivery of HBB-tdTomato and IL2RG-GFP rAAV6 donors with Cas9 RNP targeting both genes produced 10.2% double positive GFPhigh/tdTomatohigh HSPCs.
source: We therefore co-delivered HBB-tdTomato and IL2RG-GFP rAAV6 donors with Cas9 RNP targeting both genes. This strategy produced 10.2% double positive GFPhigh/tdTomatohigh HSPCs compared to 0.1% for the AAV only control sample (Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: AAV only control samples showed 0.1% double positive GFPhigh/tdTomatohigh HSPCs for di-genic targeting.
source: This strategy produced 10.2% double positive GFPhigh/tdTomatohigh HSPCs compared to 0.1% for the AAV only control sample (Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Double reporterhigh positive populations were generated when testing other combinations of di-genic HR (IL2RG/CCR5, RUNX1/ASXL1, and HBB/CCR5).
source: We also generated double reporterhigh positive populations when testing other combinations of di-genic HR (IL2RG/CCR5, RUNX1/ASXL1, and HBB/CCR5) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1c.

claim: Double reporterhigh positive cells sorted at day four post-electroporation remained 94% double positive for 15 days in culture for di-genic targeting.
source: Again, double reporterhigh positive cells sorted at day four post-electroporation remained 94% double positive for 15 days in culture (Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: 'In-Out PCR' on double positive methylcellulose myeloid and erythroid clones showed on-target integration at both loci in 88% of clones (57 clones analyzed).
source: 'In-Out PCR' on double positive methylcellulose myeloid and erythroid clones showed on-target integration at both loci in 88% of clones (57 clones analyzed) (Figure 3c and d).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCR genotyping data shown in Figure 3c and d.

claim: INDEL rates at HBB and AAVS1 were comparable among all four sorted populations (double negative, single positives, and double positive), with a small enrichment of INDELs in the three populations positive for the reporter.
source: INDEL rates at HBB and AAVS1 were comparable among all four sorted populations, with a small enrichment of INDELs in the three populations positive for the reporter (Figure 3e, middle panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by TIDE analysis data shown in Figure 3e, middle panel.

claim: Droplet digital PCR quantification of the translocation between HBB and AAVS1 showed frequencies ranging from 0.14–0.28%.
source: Droplet digital PCR (ddPCR) quantification of the translocation showed frequencies ranging from 0.14–0.28%, and importantly, no evidence of enrichment of the translocation was observed in the population sorted for di-genic targeting (Figure 3e, right panel and Figure 3—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by ddPCR data shown in Figure 3e, right panel and Figure 3—figure supplement 2c.

claim: No evidence of enrichment of the translocation was observed in the population sorted for di-genic targeting.
source: Droplet digital PCR (ddPCR) quantification of the translocation showed frequencies ranging from 0.14–0.28%, and importantly, no evidence of enrichment of the translocation was observed in the population sorted for di-genic targeting (Figure 3e, right panel and Figure 3—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by ddPCR data shown in Figure 3e, right panel and Figure 3—figure supplement 2c.

claim: Cloning and sequencing of PCR products spanning the translocation showed a wide variety of translocation junctions derived from different DNA end-processing products.
source: Cloning and sequencing of PCR products spanning the translocation showed a wide variety of translocation junctions derived from different DNA end-processing products (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2b.

claim: Human multi-lineage engraftment was evident in the bone marrow of transplanted NSG mice 12 weeks after transplantation for all four groups (double negative, single positives, and double positive).
source: 12 weeks after transplantation, human multi-lineage engraftment was evident in the bone marrow of the transplanted mice of all four groups (Figure 3g and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data from transplanted mice shown in Figure 3g and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Human HSPCs that have undergone di-genic HR are not enriched for translocations.
source: Collectively, these data show that human HSPCs that have undergone di-genic HR are not enriched for translocations, and maintain their multi-lineage colony forming capacity and long-term engraftment potential.
evidence: This claim is supported by the ddPCR translocation data and transplantation experiments.

claim: Human HSPCs that have undergone di-genic HR maintain their multi-lineage colony forming capacity and long-term engraftment potential.
source: Collectively, these data show that human HSPCs that have undergone di-genic HR are not enriched for translocations, and maintain their multi-lineage colony forming capacity and long-term engraftment potential.
evidence: This claim is supported by methylcellulose colony assays and NSG mouse transplantation data.

claim: Delivery of Cas9 RNPs targeting both ASXL1 and RUNX1c followed by transduction of four rAAV6 donors gave rise to 1.1% GFPhigh/mCherryhigh/BFPhigh/E2Crimsonhigh quadruple-positive cells.
source: Delivery of Cas9 RNPs targeting both genes followed by transduction of four rAAV6 donors gave rise to 1.1% GFPhigh/mCherryhigh/BFPhigh/E2Crimsonhigh quadruple-positive cells (Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1b–c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1b–c.

claim: A similar quadruple-positive population was evident when targeting all four combined alleles of HBB and RUNX1c.
source: A similar quadruple-positive population was evident when targeting all four combined alleles of HBB and RUNX1c (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e–h and Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1e–h and Supplementary file 1e.

claim: Mixed, myeloid, and erythroid colonies were formed at frequency and ratio comparable to AAV only controls for tetra-allelic targeting.
source: Mixed, myeloid, and erythroid colonies were formed at frequency and ratio comparable to AAV only controls (Figure 4b).
evidence: This claim is supported by methylcellulose colony assay data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Genotyping of colonies revealed on-target integration at both alleles at both loci in 78% of clones (73 clones analyzed) for tetra-allelic targeting.
source: Genotyping of colonies revealed on-target integration at both alleles at both loci in 78% of clones (73 clones analyzed) (Figure 4c).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCR genotyping data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Flow-cytometric analysis of individual colonies confirmed expression of all four reporters (BFP/GFP/mCherry/E2Crimson) at high levels.
source: Flow-cytometric analysis of individual colonies confirmed expression of all four reporters (BFP/GFP/mCherry/E2Crimson) at high levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1d.

claim: The total number of genetic changes in the tetra-allelic enriched population is six: two endogenous genes inactivated (both alleles of each gene) plus the addition of four different transgenes.
source: The total number of genetic changes in this enriched population, which could be used for synthetic biology purposes is six: two endogenous genes inactivated (both alleles of each gene) plus the addition of four different transgenes (represented in our experiment by four genes encoding different fluorescent proteins).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental design of tetra-allelic targeting.

claim: Tri-genic targeting of HSPCs at IL2RG, HBB, and CCR5 resulted in 4.1% triple-positive cells at day four post-electroporation.
source: To validate that our methodology could multiplex HR in HSPCs in more than two genes simultaneously, we electroporated HSPCs with RNPs targeting HBB, CCR5, and IL2RG, and then transduced them with gene-specific rAAV6 donors (HBB-tdTomato, CCR5-tNGFR, IL2RG-GFP) (for schematic see Figure 4—figure supplement 2a). At day four post-electroporation, 4.1% of HSPCs were triple-positive (Figure 4d and Figure 4—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4d and Figure 4—figure supplement 2b.

claim: 'In-Out PCR' on gDNA from myeloid and erythroid colonies derived from tri-genic targeted population showed that 78% (27 clones analyzed) had an integration event at all 3 loci.
source: 'In-Out PCR' on gDNA from myeloid and erythroid colonies derived from this population showed that 78% (27 clones analyzed) had an integration event at all 3 loci, indicating at least mono-allelic integrations at each targeted locus (Figure 4e).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCR genotyping data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: 85% of clones with tri-genic integrations were modified on all alleles either by biallelic integration or INDELs on the non-integrated allele that were mostly disruptive.
source: Further analyses showed that 85% of these clones with tri-genic integrations were modified on all alleles either by biallelic integration or INDELs on the non-integrated allele that were mostly disruptive (Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by genotyping data shown in Supplementary file 1d.

claim: Targeting at another combination of three genes (RUNX1/HBB/ASXL1) showed 2.9% triple-positive cells.
source: Targeting at another combination of three genes (RUNX1/HBB/ASXL1) showed 2.9% triple-positive cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2c–e), and collectively, tri-genic targeting experiments yielded an average of 4.5% triple-positive cells, with the highest frequency of 14% (N = 5) (Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2c–e.

claim: Tri-genic targeting experiments yielded an average of 4.5% triple-positive cells, with the highest frequency of 14% (N = 5).
source: Targeting at another combination of three genes (RUNX1/HBB/ASXL1) showed 2.9% triple-positive cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2c–e), and collectively, tri-genic targeting experiments yielded an average of 4.5% triple-positive cells, with the highest frequency of 14% (N = 5) (Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Supplementary file 1e.

claim: Only a minor, non-statistically significant decrease in cell viability (p=0.333) was observed when targeting three genes compared to one.
source: We observed similar proliferation rates comparing modified and unmodified cells (data not shown) and only a minor, non-statistically significant decrease in cell viability (p=0.333) when targeting three genes compared to one (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by viability data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Tetra-genic HR targeting (HBB, CCR5, ASXL1, RUNX1) resulted in 1% of cells being reporterhigh positive for all four reporters after four days in culture.
source: Finally, we targeted HSPCs for tetra-genic HR (HBB, CCR5, ASXL1, RUNX1) and found after four days in culture that 1% of cells were reporterhigh positive for all four reporters (Figure 4f).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: Targeting the same four genes with other combinations of reporter genes gave 0.41% and 0.78% tetra-genic targeting frequencies in the total cell population.
